entries.subject: Disc-resolved images or interferometric imaging of Beta Pictoris
entries.finding: The star is 0.736 mas across (Di Folco et al. 2004), 14% resolved by VLTI/VINCI at 140 m; the OiDB holds only level-0 to level-2 visibilities of it from PIONIER, GRAVITY, MATISSE, AMBER and MIDI, none published as a surface image. The sphere carries the colour of its Gaia spectrum only.
entries.revisitWhen: A reconstructed image of the star's surface is published, or public calibrated interferometry resolves it in more than a few beams.

entries.subject: Stellar radius: interferometric diameter against seismic and Gaia values
entries.finding: Adopted the VLTI/VINCI limb-darkened diameter 0.736 +/- 0.015 +/- 0.012 mas (Di Folco et al. 2004) at the Gaia DR3 distance: 1.554 solar radii. Zwintz et al. (2019) derive 1.538 +/- 0.040 from the same diameter at the Hipparcos parallax and 1.497 +/- 0.025 from their seismic model; Gaia DR3 FLAME gives 1.568 and GSP-Phot 1.574. The measured diameter is kept over the model values.

entries.subject: Limb darkening of the sphere
entries.finding: No image measures this star's limb, so the sphere is darkened by the quadratic V-band law Claret and Bloemen (2011) compute from ATLAS model atmospheres, interpolated to 8090 K and log g 4.30 between the grid nodes at 8000 and 8250 K, 4.0 and 4.5: a model, labelled as one in the lens text.

entries.subject: Spin axis and rotation period of the star
entries.finding: Kraus et al. (2020) measure the spin axis in projection with GRAVITY (aligned with the disc and planet b's orbit to 3 +/- 4 degrees) and Zwintz et al. (2019) fit a near equator-on inclination and 27% of break-up from the pulsations, but no rotation period is published, so the display axis is celestial north.
entries.revisitWhen: A rotation period of the star is measured.

entries.subject: The debris disc: HST/STIS in visible light (Ren et al. 2023 deposit) and JWST/NIRCam MASK335R at 2.1 and 4.1 micrometres (programme 4758)
entries.finding: Drawn as the attached volume beta-pictoris-disc with two lenses: the Hubble image from 16 to 82 au, where planet d orbits, and the JWST images from 49 to 126 au. JWST programme 1411's F182M image behind the smaller MASK210R coronagraph was checked for the inner disc and not used: MAST's automatic subtraction leaves speckle out to about 1.5 arcseconds and planet b stands only 2.7 times above the scatter around it. See that package's ledger and README.
